name: Timolol
route_note: eye drops or gel once or twice daily; oral tablets for hypertension and migraine prophylaxis

discovery.note: A thiadiazole-substituted propanolamine beta blocker without intrinsic sympathomimetic or membrane-stabilising activity.

tagline: First beta-blocker eye drop for glaucoma, also used after heart attack
summary: Timolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist. As eye drops it lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humour production and was a mainstay of glaucoma therapy from 1978. Orally it was one of the first beta blockers shown to reduce death after myocardial infarction. Systemic absorption from drops can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia.
mechanism: Timolol competitively blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors. In the ciliary body epithelium, beta-2 blockade reduces cyclic AMP-dependent aqueous humour secretion, lowering intraocular pressure by about 20–30%.

Systemically, beta-1 blockade slows heart rate and reduces contractility and renin release, lowering blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand. Drops drain through the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed without first-pass metabolism, so systemic beta blockade can occur.

history.title: Timoptic
history.detail: FDA approves timolol eye drops, the first beta blocker for glaucoma.

history.title: Norwegian Multicenter Study
history.detail: Oral timolol after myocardial infarction reduces mortality and reinfarction (NEJM).

history.title: Cosopt
history.detail: A fixed combination of dorzolamide and timolol is approved in the US.

history.title: Infantile haemangioma
history.detail: Reports of topical timolol shrinking superficial infantile haemangiomas lead to widespread off-label use.

pk.bioavailability: about 60% oral; systemic absorption after ocular use

facts: Pressing on the inner corner of the eye after instillation (punctal occlusion) reduces systemic absorption.
